theme: Every Voice Has Its Own Conch
hindi: हे पृथ्वी के स्वामी (धृतराष्ट्र)! राजा द्रुपद, द्रौपदी के पाँचों पुत्रों और महाबाहु अभिमन्यु (सुभद्रा के पुत्र) ने भी सब ओर से अपने-अपने अलग-अलग शंख बजाए।
english: O Lord of the Earth, King Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra, Abhimanyu, all blew their own conches, each one separately.
deeper: Sanjaya is describing the battlefield to the blind king Dhritarashtra. He calls him pṛithivī-pate, “Lord of the Earth”. The king is very powerful, yet he must hear about the war from someone else. Sanjaya keeps naming the warriors one by one, as if to say, “Listen carefully. This is who stands on the other side.”

The verse names an older king, Drupada, along with the young sons of Draupadi and Abhimanyu. So elders and youngsters are standing together in one team. The words pṛithak pṛithak, “separately, each one”, tell us that each person blew their own conch. Nobody copied anyone. Each sound was different, yet all of them rose for the same purpose.

The gentle lesson is that a strong team is not made of people who are all the same. It is made of people who each bring their own voice, their own courage and their own effort. Our own “conch” is whatever we are good at: our kindness, our singing, our drawing, our honesty. Every child has one, and it matters.
words: from all sides, all of them
O Lord of the Earth (addressing Dhritarashtra)
separately, each one on their own
background: The great war of Kurukshetra is about to begin. Blind King Dhritarashtra has asked his minister Sanjaya what is happening on the battlefield (1.1). Sanjaya describes both armies. Then Bhishma blows his conch, and the whole Kaurava army answers with a roar of horns and drums.

Then the Pandava side replies. Krishna and Arjuna blow their divine conches (1.15), and Yudhishthira, Nakula and Sahadeva blow theirs (1.16). Next, other great warriors such as the king of Kashi, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata and Satyaki join in (1.17). In this verse, Sanjaya adds Drupada, Draupadi’s sons and young Abhimanyu to the list.
lessons: Every person has their own voice
Each warrior blew a separate conch, just as each of us has our own special talent.
Young and old can be one team
Elder Drupada and young Abhimanyu stood side by side for the same cause.
Nobody waited for someone else to start. Each person sounded their own conch.
Many different sounds together became a mighty, united call.
Sanjaya noticed and named everyone. Paying attention to others is a kind of respect.
examples: Meera plays the flute, Arjun plays the drums and Sana plays the harmonium. Each sound is different, but together the school band makes lovely music.
Ravi bowls fast, Tanvi bats well and little Kabir fields sharply. When each player does their own job, the team wins together.
Some children sweep, some wipe the board and some arrange the benches. Nobody waits to be told, and the room shines in five minutes.
Dadi tells the recipe and ten-year-old Anaya stirs the pot. The old and the young cook one meal together.
One child draws the river, another paints the mountains and another colours the sky. Every part is different, and the whole picture is beautiful.
Dev knows the answer in class but feels shy. He remembers that his voice counts, raises his hand and shares it.
In Pooja’s building, the children make rangoli, hang lanterns and share sweets. Every small job adds to the festival.
In a group project, Imran listens to everyone’s idea before choosing. People feel valued when someone listens, just as Sanjaya listed every warrior.

story.title: Abhimanyu Learns Before He Is Born
paras: In the Mahabharata, Abhimanyu was the brave young son of Arjuna and Subhadra. The tradition says that while he was still in his mother’s womb, Arjuna was telling Subhadra about a difficult battle formation called the chakravyuha, a spinning wheel of soldiers.
Little Abhimanyu listened so carefully that he learned how to enter the chakravyuha. But Subhadra fell asleep before Arjuna reached the part about how to come out, so that part was never heard.

Years later, on the battlefield, Abhimanyu, now a mighty-armed young warrior, blew his own conch with the Pandavas. When the chakravyuha was formed, he bravely stepped in, because he alone, besides Krishna, Arjuna and a few others, knew how to enter it. But he had never learned the way out. The story is remembered with great respect for his courage, and also as a sad reminder of how much it matters to learn something fully.
Abhimanyu’s story shows us two things. A young person can do something big and brave with their own voice. And good preparation, listening to the very end, protects us.
story.moral: Lesson: Use your own voice bravely, and listen and learn fully so that you are truly prepared.

o: Everyone’s own voice matters in a team

reel.hook: What if your small voice is exactly what your team needs?
reel.lesson: Every person has their own conch. Use your voice, and join the team.
reel.caption:
In Gita 1.18, Drupada, Draupadi’s sons and young Abhimanyu each blew their own conch. 🐚
Different sounds, one team. What is your special sound today?
Share this with someone who makes your team stronger. 💛
